implementation_notes: java.util.concurrent is the dispatcher: ExecutorService.submit()/execute() performs the hand-off to exactly one pooled thread, and ThreadPoolExecutor makes the queue policy explicit - SynchronousQueue for direct hand-off, LinkedBlockingQueue for a queue that smooths bursts (and makes maximumPoolSize moot), ArrayBlockingQueue for bounded admission with a RejectedExecutionHandler deciding the overload behaviour (Abort, CallerRuns, Discard, DiscardOldest). beforeExecute/afterExecute are the documented tracing seam. Use it when the performers are ordinary platform threads; prefer the virtual-thread variant when the workload is many short-lived, blocking, concurrent tasks.
pitfalls: An unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue silently makes maximumPoolSize useless (documented behaviour) and turns overload into RAM; rejection cannot happen because the queue never fills.
Pool threads are non-daemon by default, so a forgotten shutdown()/awaitTermination() keeps the JVM alive and hides shutdown ordering bugs.
Exceptions thrown by a submitted Runnable vanish unless the Future is inspected; the performer looks healthy while messages fail.
ThreadLocal state (including MDC and security context) leaks between unrelated messages because pool threads are reused; clear it in beforeExecute/afterExecute.
DiscardPolicy/DiscardOldestPolicy drop messages by design - acceptable for sampling, wrong for anything the sender believes was processed.

variants.name: One virtual thread per message (JDK 21+)
variants.implementation_notes: From JDK 21 the thread-per-message style becomes affordable: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts a fresh virtual thread per submitted message, so the performer pool disappears and the dispatcher is just the submission loop with the JDK's fork-join scheduler underneath. The JEP is explicit that virtual threads must not be pooled; concurrency limits must be expressed with a different construct such as a Semaphore, because a pool of virtual threads only recreates the scarce-resource model they abolish. Choose it for high-throughput, mostly-blocking workloads; keep the platform-thread pool for CPU-bound work, where the carrier count (available processors) is the real limit.
pitfalls: Pooling virtual threads defeats their purpose (JEP 444: 'should never be pooled') and reintroduces the concurrency cap the executor was meant to remove.
A virtual thread pinned inside a synchronized block that blocks on I/O captures its carrier and can starve the scheduler; replace such locks with ReentrantLock for long blocking sections.
Thread-local caches built for platform threads (one connection per thread) become one resource per message and can exhaust the downstream service.
Virtual threads have fixed NORM_PRIORITY and are always daemon: code relying on setPriority or on non-daemon semantics must be revisited.
